The Woodcutter's Daughter

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We visit a third-generation wood-cutter from Knysna with “sawdust in her veins”: Dalena Wolmarans is the last of a rare breed making her living from the southern Cape forest in a dwindling industr

Unique Selling Point:
Dalena Wolmarans loved her father and as a child she felt most at home deep in the forest where her father would cut the logs to sell to furniture makers in the Knysna area. At 21 she already had a heavy duty truck license, knew how to use a sawmill and cut rare and expensive logs of stinkwood, blackwood and yellowood and even delivered it to customers.

She has a passion for the forest and compares the individual species of yellowwood, stinkwood, ironwood, boekenhout and others that grow in the district, to having individual temperaments - just like artists do,” she says.

She is one of only a handful of female wood-cutters that knows the different species like the palm of her hand and learnt how to survive in a man’s world. Since the loss of her father thirty years ago, she has turned adversities into a ‘forest of opportunity’ - not easy when rising costs, changing market trends, cost-ineffective and wasteful methods of producing, have taken its toll on the merchants and furniture makers alike.

Dalena Wolmarans runs two businesses in the Knysna area that were started by her father in 1958 – Adam Stander Houtverkoper and AJJ Stander Transport. Wolmarans buys indigenous hardwood timber and blackwood, cut it into planks to dry in her kiln at their Knysna premises, before selling it on to customers. On the transport side, Dalena Wolmarans runs two MAN trucks and hauls timber for local sawmills and harvesting contractors

Summary:
Dalena Wolmarans said that she loved spending her holidays on the timber trucks and, by the age of 11, her father had taught her how to pull the truck forward to save him a trip down to the hydraulic crane post. At 21, Wolmarans received her heavy duty vehicle licence and, from working as a hostess on Intercape buses she finally drove the buses. On hearing the devastating news that her beloved father had suffered a stroke she headed back to Knysna. "My father having the stroke was the first trigger of a sequence of challenges that life threw my way."

She added that, in retrospect, the challenges formed the framework of her life. "I was like the blackwood tree of the family. No-one really wanted me around, because it was the sons' place to take over. I sent out statements when that had to be done, I drove the truck picking up timber from the plantation and did the daughter's job when it was needed."

Wolmarans said that looking back at her life she can either see it as a minefield of disasters or a growing forest of opportunity. "My father died, a year later my brother died, one of my loyal workers died when cut in half during a freak accident at the neighbouring sawmill days after I had my first baby and my husband was diagnosed with cancer." She added that every setback also marked a new phase, a new challenge and a new opportunity for her.

Earlier this year Wolmarans faced a new but exciting challenge: the Department of Wood and Forest Science at Stellenbosch University under Prof Martina Meincken, asked Wolmarans to select the perfect piece of yellowood in the craftsmanship of violin. After much searching in her pile of this rare species, she found the perfect piece. “I was so surprised when I heard the beautiful sound of the violin made by Hannes Jabocs, an excellent luthier (violin maker) from Pretoria. And he told me how well it compares with the traditional violins made from the imported European Spruce wood.”


Further information:
For decades SANParks provided timber sold at auctions to merchants and furniture makers. Then in 2010 the auctions stopped. "It was a huge shock to me when SANParks told the timber buyers that they will no longer provide us with timber the way we were used to. A tender system would take over, but until that happens no interim plan has been put into place.

"A complete industry was cut off from its raw material. It has been a huge uphill battle from the day the auctions were stopped, but I am still here, cutting logs. The other day I passed the Crags where the harvested timber is kept by the tender contractors.

I looked at the devastating deterioration of the timber in the depot. I thought of the furniture makers that are gone. Gone are the people who should have replaced them. No more skills filtered down from father to son, no more woodwork at school. I was so glad that my father had died. It would have broken his heart."

Wolmarans expressed her gratitude towards the Knysna Timber Festival and said: "It gives me hope and makes me positive that, over time, the timber industry in Knysna will have a boom era again and that people will be living together as stinkwood, yellowwood and ironwood trees in one forest and will appreciate blackwood as a filler to preserve the slow-growing indigenous trees. I will feel blessed if I am still around to experience it. But until then, I will go to my sawmill on Monday and cut a blackwood tree."
Wolmarans says that the timber industry has played a significant role in the history and development of Knysna, but feels that currently there is not enough support for the small timber businesses in the southern Cape. She says that the suspension of timber harvesting by SANParks has left her short of raw materials, and has put her business under severe pressure.

Family history
Wolmarans’ father, Adam, was born in the forest in 1928 and given 2 birthdays, 22 November, the day his name was carved on a tree to note his birth and 28 November, the day Adam’s father travelled into town and registered his son’s birth in Knysna. Life was hard for the forest woodcutters. Sometimes the team would walk for days to cut down trees and would often encounter the Knysna elephants deep in the forest.

Wolmarans remembers the stories from her father: "As a boy he had to negotiate between school and work in his father's woodcutting team. Reaching standard six, he left school and became a full-time member of the team, cutting indigenous trees in the Knysna Forest. They provided products, like sleepers, to the local timber merchants, merchants who, the stories go, changed their orders the moment they saw what was on the ox-wagon."

According to Wolmarans the timber merchants of those days showed little respect to the woodcutters, always beating down the agreed price. "Grateful for any payment, the woodcutters often accepted a 'good-for' (a list of basic goods they were allowed to purchase from the merchant's store), seldom having money in their pockets." She added that her father realised that if he did not not earn physical money he would spin in a circle of poverty. Stander sold his oxen and bought a truck and managed to secure his first contract that allowed him to transport blackwood windfalls to the sawmill.

Adam was a leader in the field with immense knowledge of the forrest and so it came as no surprise that Dalena Mathee, author of "Circles in the forest" cross-checked her reference work with Adam during the research stage of the book that delves into the personal lives of the wood-cutter people.

Treatment:
We follow Dalena Wolmarans in ‘a day in the life of a wood-cutter’: From opening her small wood factory in Knysna’s industrial area to her overall in doing ‘a man’s hard-labour’ work to driving her heavy truck through the forest to go and pick up logs. We take a walk through the indigenous forest and see the giant hardwoods hundreds of years old and hear her passion for the individual species as she refers to them as ‘artists’, each with a unique personality.

The family history will form a short backdrop with photos from her father and grandfather and what the Knysna forest looked like at the time. We also bring in the anecdote of the elephants that used to roam the forest during her father and grandfather’s days.

In closing she shows us a piece of yellowood - similar to the one that made the cut for AFrica’s first violin to be made by a luthier in Pretoria as part of a project from the University of Stellenbosch’s Forest Department.

Script:


Script: The Woodcutter’s daughter
Duration: 8 Minutes
Date: 24 August 2020

Up sound

V/O Dalena Wolmarans is the owner of a sawmill and transport company in Knysna and runs her own business. This morning she has her hands full: blades have to be sharpened and logs to be cut on her trusted Wood Mizer machine.

Up sound

Dalena Wolmarans: Woodcutter - This Woodmizer is 26 years old. And this machine only had one operator in this 26 years and that is me. So I sharpen the blades and if something brakes I fix it.

Masa Kekana: This is a special skill that you have.

Dalena Wolmarans: It is the only skill I have so if you think it is special. I am honored

V/O Dalena’s roots go back three generations. Both her father and grandfather were woodcutters who made their living from the forest.

Dalena Wolmarans: My father and grandfather were born in the forest and growing up in the forest they had to walk distances to the tree that they were cutting and they stayed away for a couple of weeks.

V/O The Woodcutter era started in the 1700’s when there was a growing demand for wood in the manufacturing of ships, wagons and carts, and furniture. Skills were passed on from generation to generation: Dalena’s father, Adam left school at 14 to work full-time with his father Chrisjan. Adam knew his only chance to escape the cycle of poverty that befell so many woodcutters of the early days was to buy his own truck and transport logs for manufacturing companies in Knysna. Dalena was a gangly eleven-year-old when she started venturing into the forest with her father, Adam.

Dalena Wolmarans: I loved going to the plantations with my father because we transported pine to the sawmills. And while he was loading the truck we played around on the stacks of timber.

V/O Timber plantations were established to give the natural forest of the Tsitsikamma a chance to revive. Today indigenous forests are protected by the state and only dying trees or windfalls may be harvested under license.

Dalena Wolmarans: We are now in a part of an indigenous forest that is unique to Knysna and we are standing next to a pristine example of an Outeniqua yellowwood tree. As you can see this tree is enormous and similar trees of the same size is estimated on being about 620 years old.

Up sound - walking in forest

Masa Kekana: Dalena you are a descendant of the Knysna woodcutters - third generation - tell me how special this place is for you?

Dalena Wolmarans: Well it has got history, there is all these little stories. To me the forest is like a museum.

V/O One of the well-known stories written about the people who lived in the forest was from the pen of Dalene Matthee.

Link: Well-known South African author Dalene Matthee wrote Circles in the Forest. It is a story about a woodcutter with a restless soul who shared a bond with an elephant bull. She paid Adam a visit to cross check her facts and find out more about the woodcutters and their way of life.

Up sound

V/O Earlier this year Dalena received an unexpected call from Professor Martina Meincken from the Wood and Science department at the University of Stellenbosch in search of a piece of indigenous wood that would make a unique african violin.

Prof Martina Meincken: Forestry and Wood Science: University of Stellenbosch - When I called Dalena in February I asked her to find a few pieces of indigenous wood for me to make the violins. The wood I was looking for was a perfect radial cut without any defects of the wood species I specified and that was yellowood, blackwood and hard pear.

Dalena Wolmarans: We searched through the piles of timber then I take a photo and send it to the professor and then she rejects it. And then there was this last piece and I took a photo expecting a rejection and she said it was ok. I was delighted.

V/O Traditionally violins are made from imported Spruce or Maple wood. The property of the wood, such as the strength, beauty and colour give the instrument the specific characteristic. This project was part of a scientific study to test if our indigenous wood could be used as tone-woods in the crafting of a violin.

LINK: After all the back-and forth to find the perfect indigenous wood to make a unique African violin, yellowwood was the chosen piece.

V/O Under the craftsmanship of Hannes Jacobs, a luthier from Pretoria, a unique African violin was made. Yellowwood was used for the front and Sapele - an indigenous wood from West Africa - for the back and the neck. Bjorn Lawson, a third year music student from the University of Stellenbosch put the instrument to the test.

Bjӧrn Lawson - Violinist: So this instrument’s sound is incredible. It is made of yellowwood and sapele wood. And it is much heavier than the normal violin but the sound is so big I get gooseflesh when I do play it. The bass part of the instrument is extremely fleshy, it is very heavy, it is beautiful, but overall a very, very nice instrument to play.

Prof Martina Meincken: When we got the violin back I was very surprised with its full sound. I was a bit worried in the beginning that it would not radiate the high notes because of its wood properties but I think it sounds very, very good.

V/O For Dalena, the sound of the African violin that she contributed to is as special as the sound of the famous Stradivarius - undoubtedly the world’s most celebrated violin.

Dalena Wolmarans: They refer to the violin as the African violin but my maiden name was Stander. In my mind it is a Standevarius.

Up sound

V/O Dalena may be one of the last woodcutters of Knysna, but her grandfather’s vision for a better kind of life for his family has come to fruition in her generation.

Link: I am actually so excited right now because I have never been in a truck before and I am about to hop onto this 56 ton truck.

Up audio: Masa Kekana: Ah the truck shake.

Dalena Wolmarans: The truck shake…..are you ready to drive?

Masa Kekana: I am ready.

V/O Dalena took over driving the heavy-duty trucks the day she could get a license at age 21. She has since added another and managed to provide jobs - not least for the transport team, her husband Wollie and right-hand man Jonathan Carolos.

Up sound

V/O It’s grueling work and family life has had to be woven around the orders and deliveries - like the day her first daughter Andrea was due.

Dalena Wolmarans: Andrea was due on the 4th of July. And the 4th of July came and went and no baby so I just went on and delivered it that night...and the next morning there she was.

V/O Succeeding in business has meant Dalena could give her children a chance to choose their own path - Andrea now studies engineering at university. Her second daughter, Elizabeth is in grade 12.

Masa Kekana: We spent a day with your mom yesterday, and wow! What does it feel like to be her daughter?

Elizabeth Wolmarans: I feel it has made me very independent, it has shown me that if you really try to do something you will. And I will always be grateful for her.

V/O As fewer descendants take up the craft, the woodcutters’ numbers dwindle, but Dalena rejoices in the rich inheritance her father left behind.

Dalena Wolmarans: I had these little goals and I always hoped that he would be there to see that I met them and eventually when he died I was at peace with it.

Up sound ...violin playing
_____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Promo 1: From a stack of wood in her sawmill, Dalena Wolmarans found the perfect piece of yellowwood to craft an African violin with a unique sound never heard before.
Promo 2: Up violin music... From the Knysna forest to the concert halls, a one of a kind woodcutter has contributed to the crafting of a unique African violin.
Promo 3: Up violin music ...From the dusty floors of the sawmill rise the warm sound of Africa's first concert violin made from indigenous wood.

V/O The Woodcutter era started in the 1700’s when there was a growing demand for wood in the manufacturing of ships, wagons and carts, and furniture. Skills were passed on from generation to generation: Dalena’s father, Adam left school at 14 to work full-time with his father Chrisjan. Adam knew his only chance to escape the cycle of poverty that befell so many woodcutters of the early days was to buy his own truck and transport logs for manufacturing companies in Knysna. Dalena was a gangly eleven-year-old when she started venturing into the forest with her father, Adam. Dalena Wolmarans: I loved going to the plantations with my father because we transported pine to the sawmills. And while he was loading the truck we played around on the stacks of timber. V/O Timber plantations were established to give the natural forest of the Tsitsikamma a chance to revive. Today indigenous forests are protected by the state and only dying trees or windfalls may be harvested under license. Dalena Wolmarans: We are now in a part of an indigenous forest that is unique to Knysna and we are standing next to a pristine example of an Outeniqua yellowwood tree. As you can see this tree is enormous and similar trees of the same size is estimated on being about 620 years old. Up sound - walking in forest Masa Kekana: Dalena you are a descendant of the Knysna woodcutters - third generation - tell me how special this place is for you? Dalena Wolmarans: Well it has got history, there is all these little stories. To me the forest is like a museum. V/O One of the well-known stories written about the people who lived in the forest was from the pen of Dalene Matthee. Link: Well-known South African author Dalene Matthee wrote Circles in the Forest. It is a story about a woodcutter with a restless soul who shared a bond with an elephant bull. She paid Adam a visit to cross check her facts and find out more about the woodcutters and their way of life. Up sound V/O Earlier this year Dalena received an unexpected call from Professor Martina Meincken from the Wood and Science department at the University of Stellenbosch in search of a piece of indigenous wood that would make a unique african violin. Prof Martina Meincken: Forestry and Wood Science: University of Stellenbosch - When I called Dalena in February I asked her to find a few pieces of indigenous wood for me to make the violins. The wood I was looking for was a perfect radial cut without any defects of the wood species I specified and that was yellowood, blackwood and hard pear. Dalena Wolmarans: We searched through the piles of timber then I take a photo and send it to the professor and then she rejects it. And then there was this last piece and I took a photo expecting a rejection and she said it was ok. I was delighted. V/O Traditionally violins are made from imported Spruce or Maple wood. The property of the wood, such as the strength, beauty and colour give the instrument the specific characteristic. This project was part of a scientific study to test if our indigenous wood could be used as tone-woods in the crafting of a violin. LINK: After all the back-and forth to find the perfect indigenous wood to make a unique African violin, yellowwood was the chosen piece. V/O Under the craftsmanship of Hannes Jacobs, a luthier from Pretoria, a unique African violin was made. Yellowwood was used for the front and Sapele - an indigenous wood from West Africa - for the back and the neck. Bjorn Lawson, a third year music student from the University of Stellenbosch put the instrument to the test. Bjӧrn Lawson - Violinist: So this instrument’s sound is incredible. It is made of yellowwood and sapele wood. And it is much heavier than the normal violin but the sound is so big I get gooseflesh when I do play it. The bass part of the instrument is extremely fleshy, it is very heavy, it is beautiful, but overall a very, very nice instrument to play. Prof Martina Meincken: When we got the violin back I was very surprised with its full sound. I was a bit worried in the beginning that it would not radiate the high notes because of its wood properties but I think it sounds very, very good. V/O For Dalena, the sound of the African violin that she contributed to is as special as the sound of the famous Stradivarius - undoubtedly the world’s most celebrated violin. Dalena Wolmarans: They refer to the violin as the African violin but my maiden name was Stander. In my mind it is a Standevarius. Up sound V/O Dalena may be one of the last woodcutters of Knysna, but her grandfather’s vision for a better kind of life for his family has come to fruition in her generation. Link: I am actually so excited right now because I have never been in a truck before and I am about to hop onto this 56 ton truck. Up audio: Masa Kekana: Ah the truck shake. Dalena Wolmarans: The truck shake…..are you ready to drive? Masa Kekana: I am ready. V/O Dalena took over driving the heavy-duty trucks the day she could get a license at age 21. She has since added another and managed to provide jobs - not least for the transport team, her husband Wollie and right-hand man Jonathan Carolos. Up sound V/O It’s grueling work and family life has had to be woven around the orders and deliveries - like the day her first daughter Andrea was due. Dalena Wolmarans: Andrea was due on the 4th of July. And the 4th of July came and went and no baby so I just went on and delivered it that night...and the next morning there she was. V/O Succeeding in business has meant Dalena could give her children a chance to choose their own path - Andrea now studies engineering at university. Her second daughter, Elizabeth is in grade 12. Masa Kekana: We spent a day with your mom yesterday, and wow! What does it feel like to be her daughter? Elizabeth Wolmarans: I feel it has made me very independent, it has shown me that if you really try to do something you will. And I will always be grateful for her. V/O As fewer descendants take up the craft, the woodcutters’ numbers dwindle, but Dalena rejoices in the rich inheritance her father left behind. Dalena Wolmarans: I had these little goals and I always hoped that he would be there to see that I met them and eventually when he died I was at peace with it. Up sound ...violin playing _____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo 1: From a stack of wood in her sawmill, Dalena Wolmarans found the perfect piece of yellowwood to craft an African violin with a unique sound never heard before. Promo 2: Up violin music... From the Knysna forest to the concert halls, a one of a kind woodcutter has contributed to the crafting of a unique African violin. Promo 3: Up violin music ...From the dusty floors of the sawmill rise the warm sound of Africa's first concert violin made from indigenous wood. _____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for The Woodcutter's Daughter (5737) Annalise Lubbe 28 August 2020

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We visit a third-generation wood-cutter from Knysna with “sawdust in her veins”: Dalena Wolmarans is the last of a rare breed making her living from the southern Cape forest in a dwindling industr
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Dalena Wolmarans loved her father and as a child she felt most at home deep in the forest where her father would cut the logs to sell to furniture makers in the Knysna area. At 21 she already had a heavy duty truck license, knew how to use a sawmill and cut rare and expensive logs of stinkwood, blackwood and yellowood and even delivered it to customers. She has a passion for the forest and compares the individual species of yellowwood, stinkwood, ironwood, boekenhout and others that grow in the district, to having individual temperaments - just like artists do,” she says. She is one of only a handful of female wood-cutters that knows the different species like the palm of her hand and learnt how to survive in a man’s world. Since the loss of her father thirty years ago, she has turned adversities into a ‘forest of opportunity’ - not easy when rising costs, changing market trends, cost-ineffective and wasteful methods of producing, have taken its toll on the merchants and furniture makers alike. Dalena Wolmarans runs two businesses in the Knysna area that were started by her father in 1958 – Adam Stander Houtverkoper and AJJ Stander Transport. Wolmarans buys indigenous hardwood timber and blackwood, cut it into planks to dry in her kiln at their Knysna premises, before selling it on to customers. On the transport side, Dalena Wolmarans runs two MAN trucks and hauls timber for local sawmills and harvesting contractors
metadata.Summary: Dalena Wolmarans said that she loved spending her holidays on the timber trucks and, by the age of 11, her father had taught her how to pull the truck forward to save him a trip down to the hydraulic crane post. At 21, Wolmarans received her heavy duty vehicle licence and, from working as a hostess on Intercape buses she finally drove the buses. On hearing the devastating news that her beloved father had suffered a stroke she headed back to Knysna. "My father having the stroke was the first trigger of a sequence of challenges that life threw my way." She added that, in retrospect, the challenges formed the framework of her life. "I was like the blackwood tree of the family. No-one really wanted me around, because it was the sons' place to take over. I sent out statements when that had to be done, I drove the truck picking up timber from the plantation and did the daughter's job when it was needed." Wolmarans said that looking back at her life she can either see it as a minefield of disasters or a growing forest of opportunity. "My father died, a year later my brother died, one of my loyal workers died when cut in half during a freak accident at the neighbouring sawmill days after I had my first baby and my husband was diagnosed with cancer." She added that every setback also marked a new phase, a new challenge and a new opportunity for her. Earlier this year Wolmarans faced a new but exciting challenge: the Department of Wood and Forest Science at Stellenbosch University under Prof Martina Meincken, asked Wolmarans to select the perfect piece of yellowood in the craftsmanship of violin. After much searching in her pile of this rare species, she found the perfect piece. “I was so surprised when I heard the beautiful sound of the violin made by Hannes Jabocs, an excellent luthier (violin maker) from Pretoria. And he told me how well it compares with the traditional violins made from the imported European Spruce wood.”
metadata.Further information: For decades SANParks provided timber sold at auctions to merchants and furniture makers. Then in 2010 the auctions stopped. "It was a huge shock to me when SANParks told the timber buyers that they will no longer provide us with timber the way we were used to. A tender system would take over, but until that happens no interim plan has been put into place. "A complete industry was cut off from its raw material. It has been a huge uphill battle from the day the auctions were stopped, but I am still here, cutting logs. The other day I passed the Crags where the harvested timber is kept by the tender contractors. I looked at the devastating deterioration of the timber in the depot. I thought of the furniture makers that are gone. Gone are the people who should have replaced them. No more skills filtered down from father to son, no more woodwork at school. I was so glad that my father had died. It would have broken his heart." Wolmarans expressed her gratitude towards the Knysna Timber Festival and said: "It gives me hope and makes me positive that, over time, the timber industry in Knysna will have a boom era again and that people will be living together as stinkwood, yellowwood and ironwood trees in one forest and will appreciate blackwood as a filler to preserve the slow-growing indigenous trees. I will feel blessed if I am still around to experience it. But until then, I will go to my sawmill on Monday and cut a blackwood tree." Wolmarans says that the timber industry has played a significant role in the history and development of Knysna, but feels that currently there is not enough support for the small timber businesses in the southern Cape. She says that the suspension of timber harvesting by SANParks has left her short of raw materials, and has put her business under severe pressure. Family history Wolmarans’ father, Adam, was born in the forest in 1928 and given 2 birthdays, 22 November, the day his name was carved on a tree to note his birth and 28 November, the day Adam’s father travelled into town and registered his son’s birth in Knysna. Life was hard for the forest woodcutters. Sometimes the team would walk for days to cut down trees and would often encounter the Knysna elephants deep in the forest. Wolmarans remembers the stories from her father: "As a boy he had to negotiate between school and work in his father's woodcutting team. Reaching standard six, he left school and became a full-time member of the team, cutting indigenous trees in the Knysna Forest. They provided products, like sleepers, to the local timber merchants, merchants who, the stories go, changed their orders the moment they saw what was on the ox-wagon." According to Wolmarans the timber merchants of those days showed little respect to the woodcutters, always beating down the agreed price. "Grateful for any payment, the woodcutters often accepted a 'good-for' (a list of basic goods they were allowed to purchase from the merchant's store), seldom having money in their pockets." She added that her father realised that if he did not not earn physical money he would spin in a circle of poverty. Stander sold his oxen and bought a truck and managed to secure his first contract that allowed him to transport blackwood windfalls to the sawmill. Adam was a leader in the field with immense knowledge of the forrest and so it came as no surprise that Dalena Mathee, author of "Circles in the forest" cross-checked her reference work with Adam during the research stage of the book that delves into the personal lives of the wood-cutter people. Treatment: We follow Dalena Wolmarans in ‘a day in the life of a wood-cutter’: From opening her small wood factory in Knysna’s industrial area to her overall in doing ‘a man’s hard-labour’ work to driving her heavy truck through the forest to go and pick up logs. We take a walk through the indigenous forest and see the giant hardwoods hundreds of years old and hear her passion for the individual species as she refers to them as ‘artists’, each with a unique personality. The family history will form a short backdrop with photos from her father and grandfather and what the Knysna forest looked like at the time. We also bring in the anecdote of the elephants that used to roam the forest during her father and grandfather’s days. In closing she shows us a piece of yellowood - similar to the one that made the cut for AFrica’s first violin to be made by a luthier in Pretoria as part of a project from the University of Stellenbosch’s Forest Department.
